chapters.title: The Defense
paragraphs: I don't know how my accusers have affected you, men of Athens, but they almost made me forget who I am — they were that persuasive. Yet they've barely spoken a word of truth. What amazed me most was when they warned you not to be deceived by my eloquence. That they would say this, knowing they'd be exposed the moment I opened my mouth and proved myself anything but a great speaker — that struck me as truly shameless. Unless by 'eloquence' they mean telling the truth; if that's what they mean, then yes, I am eloquent. But you won't hear from me the kind of polished speech they gave. No — I'll use whatever words and arguments come to me in the moment. I'm confident in the justice of my case. At my age, I shouldn't be expected to perform like some young orator — so please don't expect that of me.

I have one favor to ask. If you hear me speaking the way I normally do — the same way I talk in the marketplace, at the money-changers' tables, and everywhere else — don't be surprised, and don't interrupt me. I'm over seventy years old and have never been in a court before. I'm a complete stranger to the language of this place. So think of me as you would a foreigner, speaking in his own way. Don't worry about my style — focus only on whether what I say is true. Let the speaker speak honestly, and the judge decide justly.

First, I need to answer the older charges and my earlier accusers, and then I'll address the more recent ones. I've had many accusers over many years who have been spreading lies about me, and I'm more afraid of them than of Anytus and his associates — though they're dangerous too. But the older accusers are far more dangerous. They got hold of your minds when you were young, telling you about some 'Socrates' who speculates about the heavens and investigates the earth below and makes the weaker argument appear stronger. These rumor-spreaders are the accusers I truly fear, because their audience tends to assume that anyone who investigates such things must not believe in the gods. There are many of them, they've been at it for years, and they caught you at your most impressionable age. Worst of all, I don't even know who most of them are — except perhaps some comic poet. I can't call them up here to cross-examine them. I have to fight shadows.

So let's assume, as I said, that I face two sets of opponents: one recent, one ancient. I hope you'll agree I should answer the older accusers first, since you heard them long before the others, and far more often.

Well then, I must defend myself and try to clear away, in a short time, a slander that has persisted for years. May I succeed, if success is truly good for you and for me! The task isn't easy — I understand that perfectly well. But leaving the outcome with God, and in obedience to the law, I'll now make my defense.

Let me start at the beginning. What is the accusation that gave rise to this slander and encouraged Meletus to bring charges against me? Here's what the slanderers say — let me put their words into a formal charge: 'Socrates is a wrongdoer who pries into things beneath the earth and in the heavens, who makes the weaker argument defeat the stronger, and who teaches others to do the same.' That's the accusation — the kind of thing you've seen in Aristophanes' comedy, where he shows a character called 'Socrates' walking on air and spouting nonsense about things I know nothing about. I don't mean to disrespect anyone who studies natural philosophy, but the simple truth is: I have nothing to do with such things. Many of you here can testify to that. Ask your neighbors whether any of you has ever heard me say a word about such matters. From their answer, you can judge the rest of the charges.

Equally groundless is the claim that I'm a teacher who charges fees. Though if someone truly could educate people, taking payment for it would be perfectly honorable. There are men like Gorgias, Prodicus, and Hippias who travel from city to city and persuade young men to leave their own citizens — who would teach them for free — and come pay them instead, and feel grateful for the privilege. I recently heard of another such man, a philosopher from Paros living here in Athens. I learned about him when I visited Callias, the son of Hipponicus — a man who has spent a fortune on Sophists. Knowing he had sons, I asked him: 'Callias, if your sons were colts or calves, we'd have no trouble finding someone to train them — a horse trainer or farmer who'd improve them. But they're human beings. Who are you thinking of hiring? Is there anyone who understands human excellence?'

'Have you thought about it, since you have sons? Is there anyone?' 'There is,' he said. 'Who? Where is he from? What does he charge?' 'Evenus of Paros,' he replied. 'Five minae.' Lucky Evenus, I thought, if he really has this wisdom and teaches it at such a reasonable price. If I had the same ability, I'd be quite proud. But the truth is, I have no such knowledge.

Some of you may respond: 'Fine, Socrates, but what is the source of these accusations? There must have been something unusual about your behavior. All these rumors wouldn't have arisen if you were like everyone else. Tell us what's really going on — we don't want to judge you unfairly.' That seems like a fair challenge, so I'll try to explain what's given me this reputation. Please listen carefully. Some of you may think I'm joking, but I assure you I'll tell you the complete truth. Men of Athens, this reputation of mine comes from a certain kind of wisdom I possess. What kind of wisdom? Perhaps the kind that a human being can actually achieve — in that sense, I might be wise. But the men I just mentioned may possess a superhuman wisdom that I can't describe, because I don't have it. Anyone who says I do is lying. And please don't interrupt me, even if what I say sounds outrageous. The words aren't really mine — I'll point you to a trustworthy witness: the god at Delphi. He'll tell you about my wisdom, if I have any.

You knew Chaerephon — he was a longtime friend of mine, and a friend of yours too. He shared your exile and returned with you. Chaerephon was impulsive in everything he did, and one day he went to Delphi and dared to ask the oracle — please don't interrupt — whether anyone was wiser than me. The priestess answered that no one was wiser. Chaerephon is dead, but his brother, who is here in court, can confirm this.

Why do I mention this? Because I want to explain the source of my bad reputation. When I heard the oracle's answer, I thought: What can the god mean? What's his riddle? I know I have no wisdom, great or small. What does he mean by calling me the wisest? He's a god — he can't lie. After thinking about it for a long time, I came up with a way to test the claim. I thought: if I can find someone wiser than myself, I can go back to the oracle with proof. So I went to someone with a reputation for wisdom — a politician, whose name I won't mention — and examined him. The result was this: as I talked with him, I realized he wasn't really wise, though many people thought he was, and he certainly thought so himself. When I tried to show him this, he came to hate me, and so did everyone who overheard us. As I left, I thought: well, neither of us really knows anything worthwhile, but at least I'm better off than he is — because he thinks he knows when he doesn't, while I neither know nor think I know.

In that particular respect, I seem to have a slight advantage. Then I went to another man with even higher pretensions to wisdom, and reached exactly the same conclusion. I made another enemy of him, and many others too.

After that, I went from one person to another, aware of the hostility I was provoking and regretting it. But I felt I had to put God's word first. So I went to everyone who seemed wise and tried to understand the oracle. I swear to you — the result was this: the men with the greatest reputations turned out to be the most foolish, while those considered less important were actually wiser and better. Let me tell you about my wanderings and labors. After the politicians, I went to the poets — writers of tragedies, dithyrambs, and other works. I took some of their most elaborate passages and asked them to explain what they meant, hoping to learn something from them. I'm almost ashamed to admit the truth: virtually anyone present could have explained their poetry better than they did. I realized that poets don't write from wisdom but from a kind of genius and inspiration — like prophets who say beautiful things without understanding what they mean.

The poets were in much the same situation as the politicians. And because of their poetic talent, they believed themselves to be the wisest people in all sorts of other areas where they actually weren't wise at all. So I left them, considering myself superior for the same reason I was superior to the politicians.

Finally I went to the craftsmen. I was aware that I knew practically nothing, and I was sure they knew many things — and I was right. They did know things I didn't, and in that respect they were certainly wiser than me. But I noticed that even the good craftsmen made the same mistake as the poets: because they excelled at their craft, they thought they understood all sorts of higher matters too. This flaw overshadowed their genuine wisdom. So I asked myself, on the oracle's behalf, whether I'd prefer to be as I am — knowing nothing of their craft but also free of their false assumptions — or to be like them in both respects. I concluded I was better off as I was.

This investigation has earned me many bitter enemies of the worst kind, and has given rise to many slanders. People call me 'wise' because my listeners assume I possess the wisdom I expose as lacking in others. But the truth is, men of Athens, that only God is truly wise. His oracle was meant to show that human wisdom amounts to little or nothing. He wasn't really talking about Socrates — he was using my name as an illustration, as if to say: 'The wisest among you is the one who, like Socrates, recognizes that his wisdom is worthless.' And so I go about the world, obedient to the god, examining anyone — citizen or stranger — who seems wise. When I find they aren't, I demonstrate this in service to the oracle. This work consumes me entirely. I have no time for public affairs or personal business, and I live in absolute poverty because of my devotion to the god.

There's another factor: wealthy young men with time on their hands come around me by choice. They enjoy watching me examine people's pretensions, and they often imitate me, examining others themselves. They quickly discover plenty of people who think they know something but actually know little or nothing. The people they examine get angry — not with themselves, but with me. 'This wretched Socrates,' they say, 'this corrupter of the young!' And when someone asks what evil I actually do or teach, they have no answer. So rather than admit their ignorance has been exposed, they trot out the standard charges used against all philosophers: teaching about things in the sky and underground, denying the gods, and making the weaker argument win.

That's why my three accusers — Meletus, Anytus, and Lycon — have attacked me. Meletus speaks for the poets, Anytus for the craftsmen and politicians, Lycon for the orators. As I said at the start, I can't expect to clear away so much accumulated slander in such a short time. This, men of Athens, is the truth — the whole truth. I've hidden nothing. And yet I know my bluntness is exactly what makes them hate me — which itself proves I'm telling the truth. This is the source of the prejudice against me, as you'll discover in any inquiry, now or in the future.

I've said enough about the first class of accusers. Now let me turn to the second, led by Meletus, that 'good and patriotic citizen,' as he calls himself. Let his formal charge be read: it says that Socrates is a wrongdoer who corrupts the youth and doesn't believe in the state's gods, but worships strange new divinities instead. That's the charge. Let's examine it point by point. He says I corrupt the young. But I say, men of Athens, that Meletus is the wrongdoer — he pretends to be serious when he's really being reckless, dragging people into court over matters he's never genuinely cared about. I'll try to prove this to you.
Come here, Meletus, and let me ask you a question. You care deeply about improving the young, don't you?
Yes, I do.

Then tell the court who improves them. You must know, since you've taken such trouble to identify their corrupter and bring me to trial. Speak up — who improves them? You see, Meletus? You're silent. You have nothing to say. Isn't that rather disgraceful — proof, really, that you don't care about this matter at all? Come on, friend — who improves the young?
The laws.
That's not what I'm asking. I want to know which person — someone who, first of all, knows the laws.
The judges, Socrates — the ones here in court.
You're saying the judges can instruct and improve the young?
Absolutely.
All of them, or only some?
All of them.
Well, that's wonderful news! Plenty of improvers! And what about the audience — do they improve the young too?
Yes, they do.
And the senators?
Yes, the senators too.
What about the members of the assembly — do they corrupt the young? Or do they also improve them?
They improve them.
So every single Athenian improves and elevates the young — everyone except me? I alone corrupt them? Is that really what you're saying?
That is exactly what I'm saying.

That would make me very unfortunate indeed. But let me ask you this: what about horses? Does one person harm them while everyone else does them good? Isn't it the exact opposite? Only one person — the horse trainer — does them good, while most people who handle them cause harm. Isn't that true, Meletus, of horses and all other animals? Of course it is. How happy the young would be if only one person corrupted them and everyone else improved them! But you, Meletus, have shown clearly enough that you've never given the young a moment's thought. Your carelessness is obvious in the very charges you bring against me.

Now, Meletus, let me ask you another question — by Zeus, I will. Is it better to live among good citizens or bad ones? Answer me, friend — it's not a difficult question. Don't good people benefit their neighbors, and bad people harm them?
Certainly.
Is there anyone who would rather be harmed than helped by the people around him? Answer — the law requires it. Does anyone want to be harmed?
Certainly not.
When you accuse me of corrupting the young, do you claim I do it intentionally or unintentionally?
Intentionally.

But you've just admitted that good people benefit their neighbors and bad people harm them. Am I really so ignorant that I don't know this — that if I corrupt the people around me, they'll likely harm me in return? Yet you say I corrupt them on purpose? You'll never convince anyone of that. Either I don't corrupt them at all, or I do it unintentionally. Either way, your charge fails. If I'm doing it unintentionally, the law doesn't recognize unintentional offenses. You should have taken me aside privately to correct me — if I'd been shown my mistake, I would have stopped. But you refused to teach me. Instead you brought me here — to a place of punishment, not instruction.

Even so, men of Athens, it's quite clear that Meletus has never cared about any of this. But tell me, Meletus: how exactly am I supposed to corrupt the young? According to your indictment, I teach them not to believe in the gods the city recognizes, but to worship other new divinities instead. Is that the corruption you mean?
Yes, that's exactly what I mean.

Then by those very gods we're discussing, Meletus, explain yourself more clearly to me and the court. I can't tell whether you're saying I teach people to believe in some gods — meaning I do believe in gods, just not the city's gods — or whether you're saying I'm a complete atheist who teaches atheism.
The latter. You are a complete atheist.
What an extraordinary claim! Do you really think I don't believe in the sun and the moon as gods, like other people?
I assure you, judges, he doesn't — he says the sun is a stone and the moon is earth.

My friend Meletus, you seem to think you're accusing Anaxagoras! You must have a low opinion of the judges if you think they don't know that these theories come from Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, whose books are full of them. You can find them at the theater for a drachma at most. The young would laugh at me if I tried to pass off these ideas as my own. So really, Meletus — you think I believe in no god at all?
By Zeus, you believe in absolutely none.

No one will believe you, Meletus — and I'm pretty sure you don't believe it yourself. Men of Athens, I can't help thinking Meletus is being reckless and arrogant, that he drafted this indictment out of sheer brazenness. He's set himself a riddle: 'Will the wise Socrates catch my contradiction, or will I fool him and everyone else?' Because he clearly contradicts himself — it's as if he said, 'Socrates is guilty of not believing in gods, yet also of believing in gods.' That's not the behavior of a serious person.
I'd like you, men of Athens, to help me examine this contradiction. And Meletus, please answer. And I ask the audience to remember my request not to interrupt if I speak in my usual way.

Has any person ever believed in human activities without believing in humans? ... I wish, men of Athens, that Meletus would just answer instead of constantly trying to interrupt. Has anyone ever believed in horsemanship without believing in horses? Or in flute-playing without believing in flute-players? No one ever has. But answer this next question: can a person believe in spiritual agencies without believing in spirits?
He cannot.

How fortunate that the court got you to answer! Now, in your indictment you swear that I teach and believe in spiritual agencies — whether new or old doesn't matter. The point is: I believe in spiritual agencies. And if I believe in spiritual beings, how can I not believe in spirits or demigods? I must. And what are spirits or demigods? Aren't they gods, or the children of gods?
Certainly they are.

This is the ridiculous contradiction I mentioned: you claim demigods are children of gods, yet you say I don't believe in gods — while also saying I believe in demigods, who are gods' children. It's as absurd as claiming mules exist while denying the existence of horses and donkeys. This nonsense, Meletus, could only have been intended to test me. You had nothing real to accuse me of. No one with the slightest understanding will be convinced that a person can believe in divine and supernatural beings yet not believe in gods, demigods, and heroes.

I've said enough to answer Meletus. No elaborate defense is needed. But I know all too well that I've made many enemies, and that's what will destroy me — not Meletus or Anytus, but the world's envy and malice. This force has killed many good people and will kill many more. There's no danger of me being the last.

Someone may ask: 'Aren't you ashamed, Socrates, of living in a way that might bring you to an untimely end?' I would answer fairly: you're wrong to think that. A person who is good for anything shouldn't calculate the chance of living or dying; they should consider only whether in what they're doing they are acting rightly or wrongly — playing the part of a good person or a bad one. By your logic, the heroes who fell at Troy weren't worth much, and above all the son of Thetis, who despised danger altogether compared with disgrace. When he was eager to slay Hector, his goddess mother said to him that if he avenged his companion Patroclus and killed Hector, he would die himself — 'Fate,' she said, in these or similar words, 'waits for you next after Hector.' Receiving this warning, he utterly despised danger and death, fearing instead to live in dishonor and fail to avenge his friend. 'Let me die forthwith,' he replied, 'and be avenged on my enemy, rather than remain here by the beaked ships, a laughing-stock and a burden on the earth.' Did Achilles give any thought to death and danger? Wherever a person's place is — whether chosen or assigned by a commander — that is where they ought to remain in the hour of danger, thinking not of death but only of disgrace. And this, men of Athens, is a true saying.

It would be strange indeed, men of Athens, if I — who stood my ground at Potidaea, Amphipolis, and Delium when my generals placed me there, facing death like any other soldier — were now to desert my post out of fear of death, when God himself has stationed me to live as a philosopher, examining myself and others. That would truly be strange, and would justify charging me with denying the gods — disobeying the oracle out of fear. Fearing death is nothing but the pretense of wisdom — pretending to know what we don't know. No one knows whether death might be the greatest of all blessings. Yet people fear it as if they knew it to be the greatest evil. Isn't this the most shameful kind of ignorance — thinking you know what you don't? In this one respect, I may be wiser than most: while I know almost nothing about death, I don't pretend to know. But I do know that injustice and disobedience to a higher authority — whether God or human — is evil and dishonorable. I will never choose a possible good over a certain evil.

So if you let me go now, not persuaded by Anytus — who said that since I had been prosecuted I must be put to death, or else I ought never to have been prosecuted at all, and that if I escape now your sons will all be ruined by listening to my words — if instead you said to me: 'Socrates, this time we will not heed Anytus, and you shall be released, but on one condition: you are not to enquire and speculate in this way any more, and if you are caught doing so again you shall die' — if this were the condition on which you released me, I would reply: Men of Athens, I honor and love you, but I shall obey God rather than you. As long as I have life and strength, I will never cease from practicing and teaching philosophy, exhorting anyone I meet and saying to them in my usual way: 'My friend — a citizen of the great and mighty and wise city of Athens — are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honor and reputation, and caring so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul, which you never regard at all?' And if the person I'm arguing with says 'Yes, but I do care,' I don't let them go at once; I proceed to interrogate and examine and cross-examine them, and if I think they have no virtue in them but only claim to, I reproach them for undervaluing the greater and overvaluing the less.

I will say the same to everyone I meet — young and old, citizen and foreigner — but especially to my fellow Athenians. This is God's command, and I believe no greater good has come to this city than my service to God. All I do is go around urging you — every one of you — not to worry about your bodies or your wealth, but first and foremost about the improvement of your soul. Virtue doesn't come from money; rather, from virtue comes money and every other good thing, both for individuals and for the state. If this teaching corrupts the young, then I'm guilty. But if anyone says my teaching is different from this, they're lying. So, men of Athens, whether you follow Anytus's advice or not — whether you acquit me or convict me — know that I will never change my ways, not even if I have to die many times over.

Men of Athens, don't interrupt — hear me out. I have more to say that you may want to protest, but I believe hearing me will do you good. I want you to know that if you kill someone like me, you'll harm yourselves more than me. Meletus and Anytus can't truly hurt me — a worse person can't harm a better one. They might kill me, exile me, or strip me of my rights, and they might think they're inflicting great harm. But I disagree. The evil of unjustly taking another person's life is far greater than any harm done to the victim.

I'm not arguing for my own sake now, men of Athens, but for yours — so that you don't sin against God by condemning his gift to you. If you kill me, you won't easily find a replacement. I am — if I may use a ridiculous comparison — like a gadfly attached to the state by God. The state is like a great, noble horse that is sluggish because of its size and needs to be stirred into action. I am that gadfly — constantly landing on you, waking you up, persuading you, challenging you, all day long, everywhere. You won't easily find another like me. I'd advise you to spare me. You might be annoyed — like someone suddenly woken from sleep — and swat me dead, as Anytus suggests. Then you'd sleep peacefully for the rest of your lives, unless God, in his care for you, sent another gadfly. That I was sent by God, you can see from this: no ordinary person would neglect all their own affairs for all these years, patiently suffering poverty, just to come to each of you individually like a father or older brother, urging you to care about virtue.

If I had been making money from this, or if my advice came with a fee, there would be some explanation. But as you can see, not even my accusers dare claim I've ever sought or accepted payment. And I have a sufficient witness: my poverty.

You might wonder why I go around advising people privately instead of stepping into public life to advise the state. Here's why. You've heard me speak of an inner sign — a kind of divine voice — that has come to me since childhood. It always stops me from doing something, but never tells me what to do. This is what has kept me out of politics. And rightly so. I am certain, men of Athens, that if I had entered politics, I would have died long ago without doing any good for you or myself. The truth is that no person who honestly opposes the many lawless acts committed in any state will survive for long. Anyone who truly fights for justice must do so as a private citizen, not a public figure, if they want to live even a short while.

I can prove this with actions, not just words. Let me tell you something from my own life. The only public office I ever held was that of senator. When my tribe, Antiochis, presided over the trial of the generals who had failed to recover the bodies of the dead after the battle of Arginusae, you proposed to try them collectively — which was illegal, as everyone later agreed. I was the only presiding officer who opposed the illegality. I voted against you. The orators threatened to impeach and arrest me, and you shouted for them to do it. But I chose to stand with the law and justice, and risk imprisonment and death, rather than join you in injustice. That was under the democracy. Later, when the Thirty Tyrants were in power, they ordered me and four others to bring Leon of Salamis to be executed.

This was typical of the commands the Thirty issued — they wanted to involve as many people as possible in their crimes. But I showed, not just in words but in action, that I cared nothing for death — my only concern was never to do anything unjust or unholy. The threat of that oppressive regime didn't frighten me into wrongdoing. When we left the meeting hall, the other four went to Salamis and arrested Leon. I went quietly home. I might have been killed for that, if the Thirty hadn't fallen from power shortly after. Many witnesses can confirm this.

Do you really think I could have survived all these years if I had been active in public life and had always stood up for justice, as a good person should? Certainly not, men of Athens — no one could. Throughout my life, in both public and private matters, I have never yielded to anyone unjustly — not to those people some call my 'disciples,' nor to anyone else. I don't actually have disciples. But if anyone wants to listen to me while I pursue my mission — young or old, rich or poor — they're welcome. I don't charge fees. I'm available to everyone equally. And if anyone turns out badly or well, that can't fairly be blamed on me — I never promised to teach anyone anything. If someone claims to have received private instruction from me that others didn't hear, they're lying.

People ask: why do they enjoy spending time with you? I've already told you the whole truth, Athenians. They enjoy watching me examine people who claim to be wise. There's entertainment in it. This duty of cross-examination was given to me by God — through oracles, visions, and every way divine will has ever been communicated. This is the truth, and if it weren't, it would be easy to disprove. If I'm corrupting the young, surely those who are now grown up and realize I gave them bad advice should come forward to accuse me. Or if they won't, their relatives should speak up. I see many of them in the court: there's Crito, my contemporary, and his son Critobulus. There's Lysanias of Sphettus, father of Aeschines — he's here. And Antiphon of Cephisus, father of Epigenes. And the brothers of several men who have spent time with me.

There's Nicostratus, brother of Theodotus, who has died and can't object. There's Paralus, son of Demodocus, whose brother was Theages. And Adeimantus, son of Ariston — his brother Plato is here. And Aeantodorus, brother of Apollodorus, whom I also see. I could name many more. Meletus should have called some of them as witnesses during his speech — but he can take my spot if he wants to call them now. The truth, men of Athens, is the exact opposite of his claim. All these people are ready to support me — the alleged corrupter of their relatives. Not just the young men themselves — there might be a selfish motive there — but their uncorrupted older relatives too. Why would they support me, except for the sake of truth and justice? They know I'm telling the truth and Meletus is lying.

Well, Athenians, that's essentially my entire defense. But let me add one more thing. Some of you may resent me when you recall how, in similar situations, you begged the judges through tears, paraded your children before the court, and brought out crowds of relatives and friends — while I, probably facing death, will do none of that. The contrast might irritate you and make you vote against me in anger. If anyone feels this way — and I'm not saying anyone does — I would reply: My friend, I am a man too. I have a family, and three sons — one nearly grown, two still young. Yet I won't bring them here to beg for your pity. Why not? Not from arrogance or disrespect for you. Whether I fear death or not is a separate question. But such behavior would be beneath me, beneath you, and beneath our city. A man of my age and reputation — whether deserved or not — shouldn't demean himself like that.

Whether my reputation is deserved or not, the world has decided that Socrates is somehow superior to other men. If people who are supposed to be outstanding in wisdom, courage, or any other virtue behave this way when convicted — that's shameful. I've seen respected men act as though facing death were some terrible thing, as if they could be immortal if only you let them live. They disgrace the city. Any visiting stranger would conclude that Athens' most honored citizens are no better than women. Men of reputation shouldn't behave this way, and you shouldn't let them. You should be more willing to convict the man who stages a pathetic scene than the one who quietly accepts his fate.

Setting public opinion aside, there's something fundamentally wrong with begging a judge for acquittal instead of informing and persuading him. A judge's duty isn't to hand out favors but to deliver justice. He has sworn to judge according to the law, not according to his personal feelings. We shouldn't encourage perjury — there's nothing righteous in that. Don't ask me to do what I consider dishonorable, ungodly, and wrong — especially when I'm being tried for ungodliness. If I could sway your oaths through tears and begging, I'd be teaching you to disbelieve in the gods and would convict myself of the very charge against me. But that's not how it is. I do believe in the gods — in a deeper sense than any of my accusers. And I leave my case in God's hands and yours, to be decided as is best for all of us.

chapters.title: The Penalty
paragraphs: I have many reasons not to be upset, men of Athens, at your vote of condemnation. I expected it. What surprises me is how close the vote was — I thought the majority against me would be much larger. If just thirty votes had gone the other way, I would have been acquitted. And against Meletus specifically, I think I've clearly won. Without the help of Anytus and Lycon, he wouldn't have received a fifth of the votes, and the law would have required him to pay a fine of a thousand drachmas.

So he proposes the death penalty. What should I propose instead? What do I actually deserve? What should be given to a man who has never been idle, who has ignored the things most people chase — wealth, business, military rank, political office, all the clubs and factions — because he was too honest to survive in politics? Instead, I went where I could do the most good: to each of you individually, trying to persuade every person to care about becoming wise and virtuous before caring about personal interests, and to improve the state before seeking benefits from it. What does such a person deserve? Something good, I think — something fitting. What reward suits a poor man who has been your benefactor and who needs the time to keep instructing you? Nothing would be more fitting than free meals at the Prytaneum — a reward he deserves far more than an Olympic chariot winner. That person gives you the appearance of happiness; I give you the real thing.

I'm poor, and the Olympic winner has plenty. He gives you the appearance of happiness; I give you the reality. If I'm to suggest a fair penalty, I'd say free meals at the Prytaneum is the right answer.

You might think I'm being defiant, just as I was when I spoke about tears and entreaties. I'm not. It's that I'm convinced I never deliberately wronged anyone — though I can't convince you, because we've had too little time together. If Athenian law allowed capital cases to be decided over several days, as it does in other cities, I believe I could have persuaded you. But I can't refute years of slander in a moment. Since I know I've never wronged another person, I certainly won't wrong myself by admitting I deserve punishment. Why should I? To avoid the death penalty Meletus proposes? I don't even know if death is good or bad — why would I propose a punishment I know to be bad? Prison? Why should I live as a slave to whatever magistrate happens to hold office? A fine, with prison until it's paid? Same problem — I have no money. Exile? I'd have to be blind with love of life to think that strangers would tolerate the conversations that my own fellow citizens couldn't bear.

Someone would say: 'Can't you just stop talking, Socrates, and live quietly in exile?' This is the hardest thing for me to explain to you. If I told you that remaining silent would be disobedience to God, you wouldn't believe me. And if I said that examining life is the greatest human good — that the unexamined life is not worth living — you'd believe me even less. Yet what I say is true, even though it's hard to make you see it. I've never thought I deserved to suffer harm. If I had money, I'd propose a fine I could pay without real hardship. But I have nothing. Well — perhaps I could manage one mina, so let that be my penalty. But wait — Plato, Crito, Critobulus, and Apollodorus are telling me to say thirty minas, and they'll guarantee it. So let thirty minas be the fine — they're good for it.

No, let me reconsider. Someone would say: 'Can't you just keep quiet and go somewhere else?' This is the hardest point for you to understand. If I tell you that to do as you say would be disobedience to God, you won't believe me. And if I say that the greatest good for a person is to discuss virtue every day — that the unexamined life is not worth living — you'll believe me even less. Yet this is the truth, hard as it is to accept. I've never believed I deserved harm. If I had money, I'd propose a manageable fine. But I don't. Perhaps I could scrape together one mina. But Plato, Crito, Critobulus, and Apollodorus are urging me to say thirty minas — they'll be my guarantors. Let thirty minas be the penalty; they're reliable sureties.

chapters.title: Final Words
paragraphs: You haven't gained much time, men of Athens, and you've earned a terrible reputation. The city's critics will say you killed Socrates — a wise man (they'll call me wise to spite you, even if I'm not). If you had waited just a little while, nature would have done the job for you. I'm old, as you can see — close to death already. I'm speaking now only to those who voted to condemn me. You may think I lost because I couldn't find the right words. Not at all. What I lacked wasn't words but shamelessness — the willingness to say and do whatever would please you: weeping, wailing, begging, and all the undignified behavior you're used to hearing from others. I thought then, and I think now, that a person in danger shouldn't stoop to anything base. I would rather die having spoken in my own way than live having spoken in yours. In war and in court alike, a person shouldn't use every possible means to escape death.

In battle, anyone can save their life by throwing down their weapons and begging their pursuers for mercy. In every dangerous situation, there are ways to cheat death — if you're willing to say and do anything. The hard thing isn't avoiding death; it's avoiding wrongdoing, because wrongdoing runs faster than death. I am old and slow, and the slower runner — death — has caught me. My accusers are young and fast, and the faster runner — wickedness — has caught them. I leave this court sentenced to death by you; they leave sentenced to depravity and injustice by truth itself. I accept my sentence; let them accept theirs. Perhaps this is how it had to be. I think it's fair.

Now, to those who condemned me, I want to make a prophecy — for in the hour of death, people are gifted with prophetic power. I tell you, my executioners: the moment I'm gone, a punishment far heavier than what you've given me will fall on you. You killed me because you wanted to avoid being questioned, to avoid giving an account of your lives. But it won't work out that way. There will be more people questioning you than before — people I've been holding back. They're younger and will be harsher, and you'll be even more offended. If you think killing people will stop them from criticizing your lives, you're wrong. That escape route is neither possible nor honorable. The easiest and noblest path is not to silence others but to improve yourselves. That is my prophecy to those who condemned me.

To my friends who voted to acquit me, I'd like to talk about what has just happened, while we have time before I go to my death. Stay with me a moment — we can talk while it's still possible. I want to tell you something remarkable. Throughout my life, my divine sign — that inner voice — has constantly opposed me, even in trivial matters, whenever I was about to make a mistake. Yet today, facing what most people consider the ultimate evil, the sign didn't oppose me at all — not when I left home this morning, not when I came to court, not during anything I said. In the past, it has often stopped me mid-sentence. But today it raised no objection to anything I said or did. What do I make of this? I'll tell you: it suggests that what has happened to me is actually good. Those of us who think death is evil must be wrong. My sign would certainly have stopped me if I had been heading toward harm.

Consider it this way, and there's strong reason to hope that death is good. Death is one of two things: either it's a state of complete nothingness and unconsciousness, or it's a journey to another place where the dead reside. If it's dreamless sleep, then death is an extraordinary gain. Think about it: if someone picked the night in which they slept so soundly they didn't even dream, and compared it with all the other nights and days of their life — even a great king would find very few days or nights more pleasant than that one. If death is like that, it's pure gain — eternity becomes a single peaceful night. But if death is a journey to another place where all the dead gather, what could be better? Imagine arriving where the pretend judges of this world have no power, and finding the true judges — Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus, and every other righteous soul. Wouldn't that journey be worth making?

What would you give to talk with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer? If this is true, let me die again and again! I'd find it wonderful to meet Palamedes, Ajax, and every hero who suffered an unjust death — comparing my experience with theirs would be endlessly fascinating. Best of all, I could continue doing what I do now: examining people. What would you give to question the leaders of the Trojan War, or Odysseus, or Sisyphus, or countless others — men and women both? The joy of conversing with them and examining them would be beyond measure. And in that world, they certainly don't execute people for asking questions. The dead are not only happier than the living but, if what we're told is true, they're immortal.

So be of good cheer about death, my judges, and remember this truth: no evil can befall a good person, in life or in death. The gods do not neglect such a person. What has happened to me hasn't happened by accident. I see clearly that it was better for me to die now and be released from trouble. That's why my divine sign never stopped me today. I bear no anger toward my accusers or those who condemned me. They haven't actually harmed me, even though they didn't intend to help me. For that, I may gently criticize them.

But I do have one favor to ask. When my sons are grown, I ask you, my friends, to give them the same trouble I've given you — if they seem to care more about money or anything else than about virtue, or if they pretend to be something they're not. Challenge them as I've challenged you, for not caring about what truly matters and for thinking they're someone when they're nothing. If you do this, both I and my sons will have been treated justly.
The hour of departure has come. We go our separate ways — I to die, and you to live. Which of us goes to the better fate, only God knows.
